methodology: Wohlin et al. — Experimentation in Software Engineering, validity taxonomy

high_severity_threats.title: Structural Similarity Confounding Behavioral Similarity
high_severity_threats.description: CONTROL and EXECUTION genome dimensions are derived from control-flow structure. Programs that are structurally similar (same code, refactored versions) trivially produce similar genome components regardless of semantic equivalence. Low D(G1,G2) may reflect structural proximity rather than semantic equivalence.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Ablation study comparing full genome vs. purely structural baseline vs. purely behavioral dimensions; test on structure-preserving but semantics-changing transformations; include structurally-similar hard negatives for H6.

high_severity_threats.title: Oracle / Ground-Truth Reliability
high_severity_threats.description: H5 precision/recall is measured against a gold-standard test suite T*. The oracle is itself imperfect: Defects4J labels depend on test coverage. Bugs not caught by T* are labeled 'no regression', causing genuine SBG detections to count as false positives. Circular dependency between oracle and SBG evaluation.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Supplement with mutation-testing-confirmed ground truth (PIT/Pitest); use formal verification for small calibration set; report results split by oracle-confidence level.

high_severity_threats.title: Measurement Bias from Dynamic Analysis Instrumentation
high_severity_threats.description: Instrumentation (Valgrind, Pin) alters runtime behavior: probe effect on TEMPORAL/RESOURCE, Heisenberg effect on concurrency scheduling, shadow memory overhead. The instrumented genome differs from the native genome. Differential overhead between programs may be mis-attributed to behavioral differences.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Normalize differences, not absolute values; exclude TEMPORAL/RESOURCE when overhead ratio differs >5%; use hardware performance counters as alternative; report probe overhead as experimental variable.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: MEDIUM for CONTROL/DATA/INTERACTION; MEDIUM-HIGH for TEMPORAL/RESOURCE

high_severity_threats.title: Input Distribution Sensitivity
high_severity_threats.description: Genome G(P) = Phi(P, I) is parameterized over input distribution I. Rare-event code paths are undersampled under production distribution. H2 formally requires S to cover regression-triggering inputs; if mu_I(Delta) ~= 0, H2 fails. Different experimenters using different distributions get different D(G1,G2) values — results are not reproducible across input choices.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Report results for all 4 canonical distributions (I_U, I_prod, I_cov, I_adv); conduct input distribution sensitivity analysis; use coverage-guided fuzzing for H2/H5; pin input generation protocol in replication package.
high_severity_threats.formal_model_acknowledgment: A3, A7, OP-1, H2 formal dependency on Delta coverage

high_severity_threats.title: Non-Determinism and Execution Flakiness
high_severity_threats.description: Assumption A6 requires determinism given fixed input and environment. Violated in practice by ASLR (address randomization), thread scheduling non-determinism, Python/Java hash randomization, and network/file timing. Non-determinism creates false positive regression detections when two executions of the same program produce distant genomes.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Disable ASLR, fix random seeds, serialize multi-threaded programs; measure intra-version genome variance Var[G(P)] as noise floor; use relative TEMPORAL features; implement confidence-weighted distance D_conf (OP-3).

high_severity_threats.title: Benchmark Non-Representativeness
high_severity_threats.description: Defects4J covers 17 Java open-source projects with good test coverage — not representative of enterprise software, embedded systems, or concurrent server code. Bugs are 'confirmed-fixed' type, biasing toward detectable bugs. Java-only scope means H3 cannot be evaluated on Defects4J. Results may not generalize.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Add BugsInPy, TypeScript mutations, C/C++ CVE-verified pairs; include at least one non-library server benchmark; build dedicated cross-language equivalence benchmark for H3.

high_severity_threats.title: Generalization to Real-World Programs
high_severity_threats.description: Long-running servers have unbounded traces; timeout T_max introduces truncation bias. Interactive programs require simulated users. Programs with external dependencies have non-reproducible side effects. Micro-services have distributed execution that does not fit the single-program model. Large programs produce high-dimensional genomes that are computationally intractable.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Scope evaluation explicitly to single-process, non-interactive, bounded-execution programs; study truncation bias as function of T_max; describe scaling path via program slicing.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: HIGH (fundamental — must be disclosed as scope boundary)

high_severity_threats.title: Scalability to Large Programs
high_severity_threats.description: Graph edit distance for CONTROL is NP-hard; heap graph isomorphism for STATE is GI-hard; Wasserstein-1 for TEMPORAL is expensive. Genome vector dimension grows with program size making cross-program comparison infeasible without dimensionality reduction. Results on small benchmarks do not imply tractability on large programs.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Use approximate GED; replace exact heap isomorphism with abstract heap summaries; use LSH/sketch structures for dimensionality reduction; report scaling analysis.

high_severity_threats.title: Input Space Coverage in Practice
high_severity_threats.description: Minimum sample size N* for genome convergence is unknown (OP-1). For complex programs (compilers, parsers) even large N may not cover regression-triggering inputs. H2 is fundamentally coupled to input coverage — incomparable to static analysis on bounded programs.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Report input coverage (branch/path coverage) as covariate; use coverage-guided fuzzing as primary distribution; derive empirical N* convergence curve.

high_severity_threats.title: Behavioral Distance Does Not Capture Semantic Difference
high_severity_threats.description: D(G1,G2) = 0 does not imply P1 ≡_S P2 (acknowledged in formal model). D(G1,G2) > 0 does not imply an observable behavioral difference exists. The genome is a proxy for semantic difference with no proof of validity. Positive distance may be purely measurement noise or input distribution mismatch.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Frame all claims as 'genome distance > theta predicts behavioral difference under I'; validate D against formal equivalence checkers on small programs; report D as probabilistic predictor with calibrated confidence intervals.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: MEDIUM (fundamental — Rice's theorem; only framing of claims can be made precise)
high_severity_threats.formal_model_acknowledgment: Remark R7, Rice's theorem, Def 19 relationship statement

high_severity_threats.title: Cross-Language Behavioral Equivalence as a Construct
high_severity_threats.description: No canonicalization C_E(G(P)) can be simultaneously complete (retaining all semantically relevant features) and abstract enough (eliminating all language-specific noise). CONTROL call graph nodes use language-specific identifiers (OP-4 unresolved). DATA reflects type system differences. H3 is the highest-risk hypothesis with only theoretical support.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Resolve OP-4 before claiming H3; validate H3 on minimal testable cross-language pair first; state H3 is exploratory/preliminary.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: HIGH (OP-4 unresolved; cross-language behavioral equivalence remains an open research problem)

high_severity_threats.title: Insufficient Statistical Power
high_severity_threats.description: No power analysis exists for SBG experiments. Large intra-version genome variance (from non-determinism) reduces signal-to-noise ratio. Defects4J program pairs from the same codebase are not independent samples. Testing H5 claims (recall >= 0.80, precision >= 0.70) on a small correlated benchmark is likely underpowered.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Conduct a priori power analysis; report confidence intervals on all precision/recall/distance values; use clustered standard errors for within-codebase pairs; treat codebase as clustering variable in mixed-effects models.

high_severity_threats.title: Multiple Hypothesis Testing
high_severity_threats.description: Six hypotheses tested across 8 dimensions, multiple benchmarks, and multiple input distributions. Without multiple comparisons correction, FWER across ~72 tests makes false discovery virtually certain. A single p < 0.05 result in this family is not meaningful without correction.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Pre-register primary hypothesis and test per H1-H6; apply Holm-Bonferroni or BH-FDR correction; distinguish confirmatory from exploratory analyses; report adjusted p-values.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: LOW (fully addressable with standard statistical practice)

high_severity_threats.title: Reproducibility Across Machines and Environments
high_severity_threats.description: Genome measurements are environment-sensitive (g_R, g_T are explicitly E-sensitive). The same program pair may produce different D(G1,G2) on different machines. Regression thresholds calibrated on one machine are miscalibrated on another. Genome archives (CG-3 supply-chain use case) become stale when deployment environment changes.
high_severity_threats.mitigation: Provide fully containerized replication environment with pinned OS/compiler/runtime; report full E specification for all experiments; conduct cross-machine reproducibility study; use relative normalization for TEMPORAL/RESOURCE.
high_severity_threats.residual_risk: MEDIUM (TEMPORAL and RESOURCE retain fundamental environment sensitivity)

medium_severity_threats.title: Test Data Leakage and Benchmark Contamination
medium_severity_threats.description: Threshold epsilon and theta* selected using same benchmark used for evaluation — optimistic bias in reported recall/precision.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Strict train/validate/test split; k-fold cross-validation partitioned by program not version pair.

medium_severity_threats.title: Threshold Selection Bias
medium_severity_threats.description: Five thresholds (epsilon_stable, epsilon_detect, epsilon_xlang, theta*, epsilon_collision) have no principled derivation. Different choices can flip a result from supporting to refuting a hypothesis. Optimal thresholds are dimension-dependent but a single composite threshold is used.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Report full precision-recall curves; derive thresholds from noise floor measurement; use two-threshold decision model with indeterminate zone.

medium_severity_threats.title: Compiler and Optimizer Confound
medium_severity_threats.description: Different compiler/optimizer versions change EXECUTION and RESOURCE genome features without any semantic program change. Recompilation at different optimization levels confounds genome changes with refactoring changes.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Fix compiler version and optimization flags; exclude optimization-sensitive EXECUTION features in cross-language comparisons.

medium_severity_threats.title: Generalization Across Programming Paradigms
medium_severity_threats.description: CONTROL dimension is designed for imperative/OO programs. Functional languages express computation via HOF/closures/lazy evaluation — call graphs are unstable. Logic programs have no call graph. H3 validated only on Python/Java does not generalize to Haskell, Erlang, Prolog.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Scope to imperative/OO languages; enumerate unsupported paradigms; propose g_C reformulation for functional languages.

medium_severity_threats.title: Language and Ecosystem Coverage Limitations
medium_severity_threats.description: Validation on Python+Java only does not cover non-GC languages (C/C++, Rust), Windows syscall patterns, or memory-management paradigm differences. EXECUTION dimension excluded from cross-language comparison reduces the genome from 8 to 7 dimensions, changing the metric's semantics.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Enumerate exact validated language set; build and validate C_E canonicalization before use; test on at least one non-GC language.

medium_severity_threats.title: Individual Dimensions May Not Measure What They Claim
medium_severity_threats.description: CONTROL: dominant utility loops may mask semantic control-path changes. STATE: insufficient heap abstraction makes g_S insensitive to memory-safety regressions. TEMPORAL: conflates algorithmic complexity with hardware effects. ERROR: exception types are language-runtime-specific. EXECUTION: coverage vector is static-like, not frequency-sensitive.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Per-dimension sensitivity analysis; cross-validate with domain experts; build exception taxonomy alignment for cross-language ERROR comparison.

medium_severity_threats.title: Independence and Equal Weighting of 8 Dimensions
medium_severity_threats.description: CONTROL and EXECUTION are correlated (both from location visits). DATA and STATE are correlated (heap-stored values). RESOURCE and TEMPORAL are correlated (instruction count vs. time). Uniform weights upweight correlated dimensions and treat semantically unequal changes as equal.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Compute pairwise dimension correlation matrix; explore learned weights; consider PCA decorrelation before aggregation.

medium_severity_threats.title: Normalization Changes What Is Being Measured
medium_severity_threats.description: Normalization (Definition 22) changes D from measuring actual behavioral difference to measuring normalized-representation difference. SPECint normalization suppresses algorithmic complexity differences. OP-6 (temporal normalization across architectures) is unresolved.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Validate normalization does not suppress real differences; report raw and normalized distances separately; use relative features for TEMPORAL as OP-6 partial mitigation.

medium_severity_threats.title: Mismatched Statistical Tests
medium_severity_threats.description: D is bounded [0,1], concentrated near 0 for stable programs — likely non-Normal and skewed. Parametric t-tests on non-Normal distributions produce invalid p-values. H5's precision/recall requires McNemar or paired test against a baseline, not standalone reporting.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Report empirical D distributions first; default to non-parametric tests; compare H5 against non-trivial baseline with McNemar's test.

medium_severity_threats.title: Effect Size Not Reported
medium_severity_threats.description: Statistical significance does not imply practical significance. A result with Delta_D = 0.003 may be statistically significant but engineeringly useless. Conversely, a large practical effect may be underpowered. SBG's hypotheses make magnitude claims (epsilon <= 0.05, recall >= 0.80) that require effect size reporting.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Report Cohen's d for all two-sample comparisons; 95% CI on all precision/recall/F1 values; explicitly distinguish statistical from practical significance.

medium_severity_threats.title: Overfitting to Benchmark Characteristics
medium_severity_threats.description: The 8-dimension model design and distance function choices were made with knowledge of Java/Defects4J-style programs. The model may be implicitly tuned to OO library code, JUnit test harnesses, and specific bug patterns prevalent in that corpus.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Evaluate on a completely different ecosystem benchmark (not Java, not curated university dataset); pre-register model design before seeing benchmark results; ablation study over design choices.

medium_severity_threats.title: Aggregation Conceals Dimension-Level Failures
medium_severity_threats.description: Composite D = F(d_C, ..., d_U) with uniform weights allows passing dimensions to mask failing dimensions. Noisy dimensions (TEMPORAL, RESOURCE) dilute diagnostic dimensions (CONTROL, INTERACTION). A regression on 1 of 8 dimensions produces D = max/8, which may fall below threshold theta.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Report per-dimension distances individually; evaluate dimension-level AUC-ROC; identify which dimensions contribute to correct vs. incorrect classifications.

medium_severity_threats.title: Randomness in Dynamic Analysis
medium_severity_threats.description: Input sampling randomness, fuzzer non-determinism, and residual concurrency non-determinism make G(P) a stochastic process, not a deterministic function. Different seeds produce different genome estimates G_N(P) with non-trivial variance, especially for small N.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Fix all random seeds; run genome extraction 5+ times per version and report mean +/- std; treat genome as random variable; report genome variance as primary result.

medium_severity_threats.title: Version and Dependency Sensitivity
medium_severity_threats.description: Library dependency updates change G(P) without any change to P's source code. In longitudinal comparisons, measured genome changes between versions P^k and P^(k+1) may be attributable to transitive dependency updates, not the program's own behavior change.
medium_severity_threats.mitigation: Lock all transitive dependencies (full lockfile); treat dependency version as explicit dimension; measure genome change for fixed P across library versions to quantify library-version contribution.

low_severity_threats.title: Instrumentation Tool Version Sensitivity
low_severity_threats.description: Different versions of Valgrind/Pin/custom tracer may emit different trace formats, capture different events, or have different overhead profiles. Tool updates between experimental runs create apparent genome changes that are not real behavioral changes.
low_severity_threats.mitigation: Pin instrumentation tool version in replication package; test genome stability across consecutive tool versions before deploying tool updates.

unmitigable_threats.title: D(G1,G2) Does Not Certify Semantic Equivalence
unmitigable_threats.reason: Rice's theorem — full semantic equivalence is undecidable for Turing-complete languages; OP-2 is unresolved for all but trivial programs.
unmitigable_threats.disclosure_strategy: Always frame SBG as an empirical approximation, not a semantic decision procedure. Never claim D = 0 implies P1 ≡_S P2.

unmitigable_threats.title: Rare-Trigger Behavioral Differences Are Undetectable
unmitigable_threats.reason: No finite sample covers all behavioral differences; inputs triggering mu_I(Delta) ~= 0 bugs will never be sampled from I_prod.
unmitigable_threats.disclosure_strategy: State sensitivity bounds explicitly; measure input coverage as a covariate in all H2/H5 experiments; use I_adv to bound the coverage gap.

unmitigable_threats.title: Long-Running, Interactive, and Distributed Programs Are Out of Scope
unmitigable_threats.reason: Timeout-bounded trace extraction cannot capture behaviors emerging over long execution horizons; multi-process programs violate Definition 2's single-program model.
unmitigable_threats.disclosure_strategy: Explicitly scope all claims to: single-process, non-interactive, execution-time < T_max, no external stateful dependencies.

unmitigable_threats.title: Functional and Logic Paradigms Are Not Supported
unmitigable_threats.reason: CONTROL dimension (g_C) is definitionally OO/imperative-centric; call graphs are not meaningful or stable constructs in functional or logic paradigms.
unmitigable_threats.disclosure_strategy: Enumerate supported paradigms explicitly in the paper scope section; do not claim generality beyond imperative/OO languages without a formal paradigm extension.

unmitigable_threats.title: Cross-Language Behavioral Equivalence (H3) Depends on Unresolved OP-4
unmitigable_threats.reason: No formal cross-language procedure alignment mapping exists; CONTROL dimension g_C cannot be compared across language boundaries without it.
unmitigable_threats.disclosure_strategy: Mark H3 as exploratory/preliminary; validate only on dimensions that do not require procedure-level alignment (DATA g_D, INTERACTION g_X, ERROR g_E); do not claim confirmed cross-language genome equivalence.

key_recommendations_priority_order: 1. CL-02: Pre-register experiments and apply FDR correction before conducting any evaluation — zero cost, prevents false discovery.
2. IV-05: Measure intra-version genome variance (noise floor) before making any inter-version distance claim.
3. IV-04: Report input coverage as a covariate in all H2/H5 experiments.
4. CL-01: Conduct a priori power analysis; report confidence intervals on all metrics.
5. IV-01: Run structural-baseline ablation to disentangle structural from behavioral signal.
6. IV-02: Supplement Defects4J with mutation-testing-confirmed ground truth.
7. CV-01: Frame all claims as probabilistic predictors, not semantic certificates.
8. CV-05: Resolve OP-4 or explicitly mark H3 as exploratory.
9. RL-01: Provide containerized replication environment with full environment specification.
10. CL-06: Report per-dimension distances alongside composite D in all experiments.
